title: Exponents and Radicals — Chapter Summary
intro: Exponents give a compact way of writing repeated multiplication; radicals are their inverse, capturing the operation of taking n-th roots. This chapter develops the laws of exponents and extends them from positive integers to zero, negatives and rational exponents, and ends with the simplification of radicals and the technique of rationalising denominators.

sections.heading: Positive Integral Exponents
bullets: For a positive integer n, a^n means a multiplied by itself n times.
a is the base; n is the exponent (or index, or power).
(−a)^n = a^n if n is even and (−a)^n = −a^n if n is odd.
Five laws hold for any real bases a, b and positive integers m, n: product, quotient, power-of-a-power, power-of-a-product, power-of-a-quotient.
Each law follows directly from counting factors of a.

sections.heading: Zero and Negative Exponents
bullets: a^0 = 1 for any non-zero a; the convention is forced by the product law (a^0 × a^n = a^n).
0^0 is left undefined.
a^(−n) = 1 / a^n for any non-zero a and positive integer n.
With these definitions, all five laws of exponents extend to any integer exponent.
Negative exponents express reciprocals; e.g. 2^(−3) = 1/8 and (3/4)^(−2) = (4/3)^2 = 16/9.

sections.heading: Rational Exponents
bullets: n√a, the n-th root of a, is the unique non-negative x with x^n = a (for a ≥ 0).
For odd n, n√a is defined for any real a; for even n, n√a is undefined when a < 0 (in the real numbers).
Rational exponents: a^(m/n) = (a^(1/n))^m = (a^m)^(1/n) = n√(a^m), for a > 0.
All five laws of exponents extend to rational exponents when bases are positive.

sections.heading: Radicals and Surds
bullets: n√a = a^(1/n); n is the index (or order), a is the radicand.
When n = 2 we drop the index and write √a — the square root.
A surd is a radical n√a where a is rational and the n-th root is irrational (e.g. √2, 3√5).
Pure surd: rational coefficient 1 (e.g. √7). Mixed surd: non-trivial coefficient (e.g. 3√2).
Like surds have the same index and the same radicand; only like surds combine by adding coefficients.

sections.heading: Simplification of Radicals
bullets: A radical n√a is simplified when (i) the radicand has no perfect-n-th-power factor, (ii) it has no fraction, and (iii) no fraction has a radical in its denominator.
Like surds add by combining coefficients: p√a + q√a = (p + q)√a.
Multiply / divide same-index surds by combining radicands: (p · m√a)(q · m√b) = pq · m√(ab).
Surds with different indices: bring to a common index n = lcm(m1, m2) before comparing or combining.

sections.heading: Rationalisation of Denominators
bullets: Goal: rewrite a fraction so its denominator is rational.
Single-term denominator √a: multiply numerator and denominator by √a; uses √a · √a = a.
Two-term denominator a + b√c: multiply by the conjugate a − b√c; uses (a + b√c)(a − b√c) = a² − b²c.
Conjugate of √a + √b is √a − √b, with product a − b.

key_takeaways: Exponents give a compact notation for repeated multiplication; radicals capture the inverse operation.
The five laws of exponents extend naturally from positive integers to zero, negative and rational exponents.
a^0 = 1 and a^(−n) = 1/a^n are forced by the product law, not chosen arbitrarily.
n√a = a^(1/n); a surd is a radical with rational radicand and irrational value.
Simplify radicals by removing perfect-power factors from the radicand.
Rationalise denominators by multiplying by the appropriate factor — the surd itself for one-term denominators, and the conjugate for two-term denominators.

glossary.definition: In a^n, the integer or rational number n that tells how many factors of a we multiply.
In a^n, the number a being raised to a power.
a^0 = 1 for any non-zero a; the convention forced by the product law.
a^(−n) = 1 / a^n for any non-zero a and positive integer n.
a^(m/n) = n√(a^m), defined for a > 0 and integers m, n with n > 0.
n√a is the non-negative real x such that x^n = a (for a ≥ 0).
An expression of the form n√a using the radical sign √.
A radical n√a where a is rational and n√a is irrational (e.g. √2, 3√5).
A surd with rational coefficient 1, e.g. √7.
A surd with a non-trivial rational coefficient, e.g. 3√2.
Surds with the same index and the same radicand; only these can be combined by adding coefficients.
A radical whose radicand has no perfect-n-th-power factor, no fraction, and whose denominator (if any) contains no radical.
The expression a fraction's denominator is multiplied by to make the new denominator rational.
For a + b√c, the conjugate is a − b√c; their product a² − b²c is rational.
